content: Bill Wilson, also known as Bill W., was born on November 26, 1895, and passed away on January 24, 1971. He is best known as the co-founder of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), a fellowship of self-help groups aimed at aiding individuals in recovering from alcoholism. In accordance with AA's tradition of anonymity, Wilson is commonly referred to as Bill W. even today. His journey to sobriety began in 1934 when he experienced a profound spiritual awakening that empowered him to stop drinking. This pivotal moment led him to develop a method of recovery that he shared with others, starting with Dr. Bob Smith, the co-founder of AA, in 1935. Together, they created the Twelve-Step program, a spiritual framework for recovery, and the Twelve Traditions, which serve as the organizational principles of AA. Despite his achievements and long-term sobriety, Wilson struggled with personal demons, including compulsive behaviors and recurrent depression. In 1955, he relinquished leadership of AA to its service board, allowing him to explore alternative treatments for alcoholism. He became interested in spiritualism, niacin (vitamin B3) as a potential remedy for alcoholism, and even experimented with LSD as a means of inducing spiritual transformation. Wilson ultimately succumbed to lung disease in 1971. His wife, Lois Wilson, founded Al-Anon, a support group for the friends and family of alcoholics. When Wilson was ten years old, his father left the family permanently, and his mother abandoned him and his sister to pursue a career in osteopathic medicine. The siblings were raised by their maternal grandparents. Despite these early hardships, Wilson demonstrated determination and creativity in his youth. He taught himself to play the violin and excelled in sports after initial struggles in school. However, at the age of seventeen, he experienced a profound depression following the death of his first love, Bertha Bamford, during surgery. Wilson met his future wife, Lois Burnham, in 1913, and they became engaged two years later. In 1917, he was drafted into the army, where he had his first experiences with alcohol. At a dinner party, he drank Bronx cocktails and felt liberated from his social awkwardness, describing the experience as discovering the elixir of life. However, this marked the beginning of his dependence on alcohol. After marrying Lois in 1918, Wilson served in Europe during World War I, where he was further exposed to alcohol. Upon returning to New York, his drinking escalated, leading to his failure to graduate from law school and the eventual collapse of his career as a stock speculator. By 1933, Wilson's alcoholism had become so severe that he was hospitalized three times under the care of Dr. William D. Silkworth, who viewed alcoholism as both an allergy and an obsession. While Wilson found hope in the idea that alcoholism was a medical condition rather than a moral failing, he continued to struggle. He was warned that his condition would either lead to death or permanent institutionalization. A turning point came when an old friend, Ebby Thacher, visited Wilson and revealed that he had achieved sobriety through the Oxford Group, a Christian evangelical movement. Inspired by Thacher's transformation, Wilson sought help and was admitted to Towns Hospital. During his stay, he experienced a profound spiritual awakening, which he described as a sensation of bright light and serenity. This experience marked the end of his drinking. Encouraged by Dr. Silkworth and Thacher, Wilson began sharing his story and helping other alcoholics. Wilson initially joined the Oxford Group and attempted to help others achieve sobriety, but his efforts were unsuccessful until he adopted a new approach. Influenced by Dr. Silkworth's advice, he began focusing on the medical and psychological aspects of alcoholism, as well as his personal experiences. In 1935, during a business trip to Akron, Ohio, Wilson met Dr. Bob Smith through a mutual acquaintance, Henrietta Seiberling. Their meeting, which lasted four hours, led to Dr. Bob's sobriety and the eventual founding of Alcoholics Anonymous. The first official AA meeting occurred when Wilson and Dr. Bob helped another alcoholic, Bill D., achieve sobriety. The fellowship grew rapidly, and by 1938, there were approximately 100 sober members in Akron and New York. To spread their message, Wilson authored a book titled Alcoholics Anonymous, which outlined the Twelve Steps for spiritual growth and recovery. The book's title became synonymous with the movement itself. As AA expanded, Wilson recognized the need for a unified structure. He developed the Twelve Traditions, which emphasized principles such as anonymity, democracy, and the avoidance of power or financial accumulation within the organization. These traditions were formally adopted in 1955, when Wilson handed over leadership of AA to an elected board. In his later years, Wilson explored unconventional treatments for alcoholism, including niacin and LSD, which he believed could facilitate spiritual experiences. He also maintained a lifelong interest in spiritualism, claiming to receive guidance from the spirit world. However, he kept these activities separate from AA to avoid controversy. Despite his personal struggles, including a lifelong addiction to smoking that contributed to his death, Wilson's contributions to the field of addiction recovery were monumental. Wilson's legacy is complex. While he was a visionary leader and a synthesist of ideas from psychology, theology, and democracy, he was also a deeply flawed individual. He struggled with depression, compulsive behaviors, and infidelity. Nevertheless, his work has saved countless lives, and he is remembered as an ordinary man who achieved something extraordinary. Time magazine recognized him as one of the most important figures of the 20th century, and his creation of AA remains a testament to his resilience and ingenuity.
